name: MARSHALL IS.
tagline: Atolls at the edge of sky

flag.title: Flag of the RMI
flag.note: Blue field, orange & white bands, 24-pt star

lead: Scattered like dropped beads across the Pacific, the Marshall Islands are two chains of coral atolls so flat you can see clear across most of them. Every view is ocean — turquoise lagoons one side, open sea the other. The country holds the world record for the lowest average height of any nation, barely two metres above the waves.
geo: The Marshall Islands are two parallel chains — Ratak (Sunrise) and Ralik (Sunset) — totalling 29 atolls and 5 single islands. All 1,152 specks of land share just 181 km² of ground, less than Washington D.C., while the ocean they dot covers nearly 2 million km².

Coral atolls form as rings of reef around sunken volcanoes, leaving a calm lagoon in the middle. Kwajalein holds the world's largest lagoon — big enough to hide a city inside. The average altitude is just 2 metres, making every king-tide a genuine emergency.
animals: The real zoo here is underwater: 250-plus reef fish species weave through 300 kinds of coral. Green and hawksbill sea turtles nest on quiet beaches, and humpback whales pass through on migration.

On land, the great frigatebird rules the sky — a pirate bird that steals fish mid-air. Giant coconut crabs, the world's largest land invertebrate, scale palm trees and crack coconuts with claws like bolt cutters.
culture: Marshallese society is matrilineal — land and rank pass through mothers, not fathers. Traditional stick charts called rebbelib were used by navigators to read ocean-swell patterns between atolls, a skill unique to these islands.
Christmas, called Kūrijmōj, is a four-month community celebration of songs and feasting. Outrigger canoe building remains a living craft, and woven pandanus mats made by women are prized as gifts.
history: Marshallese ancestors arrived some 2,000 years ago, mastering open-ocean navigation. Spanish, German, and then Japanese colonial powers each claimed the atolls before the US took control after fierce World War II battles.
Between 1946 and 1958 the US detonated 67 nuclear weapons on Bikini and Enewetak — total blast force 7,000 times Hiroshima. The Marshall Islands gained independence in 1986.
wows: Bikini Atoll is UNESCO World Heritage; sunken warships from nuclear tests sit on its lagoon floor.
The Marshall Islands sits west of the Date Line, sharing a calendar day with Asia rather than nearby Hawaii.
Marshallese read ocean swells felt under the hull to find islands over the horizon — wave piloting.
The country uses the US Dollar and has no central bank — one of few nations without its own currency.
Soil on Bikini Atoll measures radiation ten times higher than the Chernobyl and Fukushima exclusion zones.
Majuro's main island is rarely wider than 300 metres — you can walk lagoon to ocean in two minutes.
Marshallese citizens need no visa to live and work in the USA under the Compact of Free Association.

myths.myth: The islands are flat, treeless deserts
myths.fact: The atolls are lush with coconut palms, breadfruit, and pandanus — vivid green rings around brilliant blue lagoons, nothing like a desert.

myths.myth: Only Bikini islanders were affected by nuclear tests
myths.fact: The 1954 Castle Bravo bomb rained fallout on inhabited atolls 150 km away, harming thousands with health effects lasting generations.
